summary:
SolKeeper is a zero login, browser-based mission simulator developed for students ages 7–12 to experience the real engineering trade-offs of running a Lunar or Martian outpost. Built in modular Vanilla JavaScript, the web application challenges young learners to survive 10 Sols on Mars (Jezero Crater) or the Moon (Shackleton Crater) by allocating a limited kilowatt power budget across Life Support, Hydroponic Food Production, and Active Radiation Shielding.

Rather than simplifying spaceflight into trivia, SolKeeper addresses the challenge through dynamic system trade offs grounded in real telemetry fetching solar flare events from NASA’s DONKI Space Weather Database and incorporating closed-loop nutrition and life support hazards from the Canadian Space Agency’s (CSA) Food Production on the Moon toolkit. When a resource depletes, an After-Action Engineering Report explains the physics behind what went wrong. This hands-on approach makes complex aerospace systems accessible, showing students how sustainable resource recycling supports both deep-space exploration and remote communities on Earth.
details:
What It Does & How It Works SolKeeper is an interactive, browser-based mission control simulator designed for young learners (ages 7–12) to experience the real engineering trade-offs of managing a Lunar or Martian outpost. Players choose between two authentic mission sites Mars (Jezero Crater) and the Moon (Shackleton Crater) and work to keep their base operational across a 10-Sol mission. Every Sol, players distribute a limited kilowatt power budget across three competing subsystems: Life Support & Water Recycling, Hydroponic Food Production, and Active Radiation Shielding. Each allocation triggers interconnected consequences (such as hydroponic crops consuming water reserves or reduced power output during Martian dust storms), requiring players to adapt their strategy on the fly.

Benefits & Intended Impact Space-themed STEM tools often oversimplify spaceflight into trivia or present data too densely for elementary and middle-school students. SolKeeper bridges that gap by turning real aerospace constraints into tangible cause-and-effect gameplay. If any critical resource depletes, an After-Action Engineering Report explains the scientific reason behind the failure in kid-friendly language rather than a generic "Game Over" screen, encouraging iterative problem-solving. Beyond space literacy, the simulator highlights how closed-loop water recycling and low-power hydroponics also help remote communities on Earth grow fresh food sustainably.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Frontend & Simulation Engine: Modular Vanilla JavaScript (ES6 Modules), HTML5, and CSS3 with custom Mission Control variables and color-coded status indicators.
  • Data & Telemetry Integration: Live REST API integration with NASA’s Space Weather Database (DONKI) (using sessionStorage caching and an offline fallback archive) alongside curated environmental and nutrition parameters from the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) Food Production on the Moon toolkit, NASA Curiosity (REMS), and the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO).
  • Version Control & Cloud Hosting: Git, GitHub, and automated static deployment via Render.

Creativity & Design Considerations

  • Zero-Friction Access: Designed as a pure client-side web application with no logins, downloads, or external dependencies so students, teachers, and judges can launch a mission immediately in any browser.
  • Authentic, Kid-Friendly Storytelling: Instead of abstract numbers, space hazards are grounded in real astronaut experiences—from NASA DONKI solar flare alerts to CSA microgravity food challenges like floating crumbs clogging air filters and "space congestion" dulling crew taste buds.
  • Focused Cognitive Load: Resource mechanics were deliberately scoped to four intuitive metrics (Oxygen, Water, Food, and Shielding) with clear visual thresholds (green/yellow/red) so young learners can grasp complex system dependencies without feeling overwhelmed.
